3776.prule: One stressed syllable per content word (and per polysyllabic function word). Stress is anchored to the lexical root, never to the noun-class prefix (gu.láar). Demarcative only; no minimal pairs.

3777.heavy: Category heading: 'Stress is on the first long vowel, else on the first syllable'; but the Kukatj entry's own annotation sets the criterion: '(QS: vowel quality, a word never consists of only light syllables)', i.e. full-vowel syllables heavy, schwa syllables light. Code key: 'QS: marginal quantity-sensitivity'. First-hand fragments (excerpt grade): Breen 1976 'The centralised vowel [ə] is very common but does not occur in stressed syllables'; Jones 2000 on Breen 1992:10-11 'the vowel of the syllable preceding a primary-stressed syllable is schwa'. No reachable source states that phonemic vowel length conditions stress; Black 1980 p. 197 only reports that e, o, a 'could be reanalysed as i, u, and a respectively plus length, which Breen (1976a) suggests could be contrastive for Kukatj'.
3777.dflt: first syllable ('else on the first syllable'); under the entry's vowel-quality criterion the default is stated to be vacuous ('a word never consists of only light syllables').
3777.prule: Second-hand (Goedemans 1998 classifying Breen 1992): main stress on the first heavy syllable of the word, otherwise on the first syllable. For Kukatj the entry's own annotation sets the weight criterion as vowel quality (syllable with a full vowel = heavy, syllable with schwa = light) and states that a word never consists of only light syllables, so the 'else first syllable' clause is vacuous. The reachable first-hand fragments agree: schwa 'does not occur in stressed syllables' (Breen 1976, excerpt) and 'the vowel of the syllable preceding a primary-stressed syllable is schwa' (Breen 1992:10-11 as reported by Jones 2000, excerpt).
3777.srule: Second-hand code only (Goedemans 1998, code Ed on the Kukatj entry, classifying Breen 1992): one secondary stress at the edge opposite the main stress (the right, word-final edge), or footing for secondary stress starts at that edge; the code does not say which, no RS ('regular secondary stresses') code is attached, and no Kukatj words are given. Breen 1992 itself not opened.

3780.dq: A word is an isolatable syllable or group of syllables with one primary stress as defined above. [p. 47] ... Beyond the word level the language is divided into intonational pause groups, each consisting of a word or group of words ending in a distinctive intonational pattern followed by a pause. [p. 48]
3780.dloc: §1.3 Stress, p. 47 (stress paragraph read; also §2 Syllable Patterns p. 48, §3 Intonational Pause Groups p. 48, §4 Dialectal Differences p. 49)
3780.heavy: The source states only the light case: 'short, i.e. V or CV'. The complementary heavy initial is VV or CVV (two-vowel syllable: identical vowels or any of the 25 vowel combinations, p. 48); there are no closed syllables in the language (syllable types V, VV, CV, CVV; CVVV in two words).
3780.dflt: Second syllable in words of three or more syllables (light initial); initial syllable in disyllables (the shift is restricted to 3+-syllable words, so a disyllable keeps initial stress whatever its weights).
3780.prule: One primary stress per word. Primary stress is on the initial syllable, except in words of three or more syllables whose initial syllable is short (V or CV), where it falls on the second syllable. Since the only syllable types are V, VV, CV, CVV (no codas), 'short' = one vowel and the retained-initial case is a VV/CVV (long vowel or diphthong) initial; disyllables are always initial-stressed.
3780.srule: Secondary stress exists but no position is given: it 'is very light and varies freely' (Richert & Richert 1972: 47). No later opened work (Richert & Hoopusu 2002; Gamudze, Hadzata & King 2013) says anything about secondary stress.

3781.heavy: Syllable weight is determined by the number of segments, or moras, in the rhyme (vowel nucleus plus any trailing consonants; a long vowel counts as two moras): light = rhyme V; heavy = rhyme VV or VC; superheavy = rhyme VVC or VCC. The final segment of the word is extrametrical, so a word-final CVC syllable counts as light and a final CVVC or CVCC as heavy.
3781.dflt: the penultimate syllable is stressed (a word of light syllables only)
3781.prule: Stress falls on the last heavy syllable of the word, where heavy = rhyme VV or VC (superheavy VVC/VCC also heavy) and the word-final segment is extrametrical (not counted for weight); if the word has no heavy syllable, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Examples: /'jisam/ 'body' (final /m/ excluded, two light syllables, penult stressed); /as'maːN/ 'sky' (second syllable is the last heavy syllable). One stress per word.

For a small number of words, stress falls on a non-initial syllable and surface tones attest a medial, rather than initial, lexical L. Examples include /daːde'aːL/ ... 'paternal re…
3781.tone: Three lexical pitch melodies (level 'mid' tone unmarked, high-falling 'high' tone, low-rising 'low' tone; Sharma 1979:110-113, 1982:12 for Punch Gojri, confirmed for Kaghani and Allaiwal). Losey analyses tone as anchored on the stressed syllable: H is assigned by default to every stressed syllable, L is lexical (from a lost voiced aspirate or /h/), and the contour (HL vs LH) depends on where the L sits relative to the stressed nucleus; 'Gojri is more like Swedish than Mandarin' (p. 65). So the language has both a weight-based stress rule and a stress-anchored lexical tone contrast; the stress rule is the catalog statement.

3782.prule: Lexically contrastive syllabic intensity inside a register-tone system; no position is computable from syllable count. Nougayrol 1999 (Phonologie, pp. 36-41) sorts the CVCV disyllables of méré and sara into three types: (1) forms without syllabic contrast, 82 % of méré CVCV disyllables; (2) CvCV, intensity on the second syllable with the first vowel reduced to schwa or elided — only eight méré terms (four numerals: mātá 'trois', məká 'six', mandé 'sept', ndētá 'huit'), seven koto terms (three numerals), and zura 'dans des proportions comparables au GM'; (3) CVCv, surface [CVC] analysed only 'dans l'hypothèse haute' as intensity on the first syllable with the final vowel elided (méré 17 %). The second parler's figures, 27 % (2nd type) and 9 % (3rd type), are given in a sentence comparing 'terme à terme avec le méré' and so belong to sara by inference. Whether a word carries intensity, and on which syllable, is a property of the lexeme (mādā 'cynocéphale' without contrast vs māta 'trois' with final intensity), so the prominence is lexical/contrastive; the majority of disyllables show no prominence contrast at all.
3782.srule: Not mentioned in Nougayrol 1999, Première partie 'Phonologie', syllabic-intensity passage (pp. 36-41) and lexicon conventions, read at Google Books grade: the intensity contrast is described only for disyllables (one intense syllable, one 'syllabe faible'); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

With the exception of loanwords and ideophones, these can all be analysed as three underlying level tones, with rising and falling tones as allotones of the level tones. 3799.quote: In this chapter, I argue that Haruai has a language internal phonological correlate of the head-dependent relation, namely that, in the absence of other factors (contrastive stress, greater stress associated with focus, that is, essential new information), dependents receive greater stress than their heads. 3800.dq: मानक हिन्दी और बांगरू दोनों में सार्थक बलाघात की सत्ता शब्द स्तर पर है [...] सामान्यता शब्द में केवल एक अक्षर पर ही बलाघात होता है (Bansal 1981: 95-96). Meaningful (contrastive) stress exists at word level, i.e. as emphasis on a word in the sentence; within the word one syllable per word is stressed and its position is predictable.
3800.dloc: Bansal, Somdatt (सोम दत्त). 1981. Mānak Hindī aur Bāṅgrū kā vyatirekī viśleṣaṇ / A contrastive analysis of Standard Hindi and Bangru. PhD thesis, Panjab University, Chandigarh. §1.9.1-1.9.2, pp. 95-96.
3800.heavy: Not defined in Bansal; by his deferral to Sharma (1958 §46-47): 'a syllable ending in a consonant is called close, that ending in a vowel is called open. A close syllable is, of course, always long' and a syllable with a long vowel is long; 'if only one is long and the rest short, the long one (wherever it may occur) is accented'; 'if a word contains more than one long syllable, the last but one, if long, is accented'; 'The last syllable is never accented, unless, of course, it is the only long syllable in the word'. Bansal's Bangru examples additionally treat final CVVC as heavier than CVV (bazār, bimār, tufān, madān, satān stress the final), i.e. a superheavy tier as in Kelkar/Ohala-type Hindi rules rather than Sharma's two-level rule (c), which would accent the CVV penult.
3800.dflt: Penult, per the Hindi rule Bansal defers to (Sharma 1958 §47e: 'In words consisting of only short syllables, the last but one is accented'); not stated for Bangru itself.
3800.prule: One stress per word, non-contrastive within the word and predictable (anumey); Bansal does not restate the placement rule but says the rule scholars give for Standard Hindi applies to Bangru (fn. 4: Aryendra Sharma, A Basic Grammar of Modern Hindi 1975 pp. 17-18). That rule (Sharma 1958 §47, read): one accent per word; if only one syllable is long (long vowel or closed syllable) it is accented wherever it stands; with several long syllables the penult if long, otherwise the nearest preceding long syllable; the final is never accented unless it is the sole long syllable; all-short words accent the penult. Bansal's own Bangru data (§1.9.3, pp. 97-98) locate the stress on the heaviest syllable: initial CVV in móṭā > móṭṭā, final CVVC over CVV penult in bāzār > bazār, bīmār > bimār, tūfān > tufān (pretonic long vowel shortened), sole heavy final in anāj > nāj, ahīr > hīr (pretonic light syllable deleted).
3800.srule: None: 'सामान्यता शब्द में केवल एक अक्षर पर ही बलाघात होता है' (normally only one syllable in a word bears stress); no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned anywhere in §1.9 Balāghāt (pp. 95-100).

3802.dq: HCE also places stress differently than Mainland English at the word level.
3802.dloc: Sec. 1.8.4 'Word Stress', p. 24; also p. 130 = ('HCE places word level stress differently compared to Mainland English').
3802.prule: No positional rule is stated. Word stress is English-type lexical stress that differs word by word from Mainland English; in Murphy's 13-item contrast list HCE stress sits further right than in Mainland English: on the final syllable (hurriCANE, moloKAI, proTEST, disCOUNT, traumaTIZE, headREST, chinaTOWN, townHOUSE, chickenFIGHT), on the penult (graduATed, weed WHAckers), or on the right-hand member of a compound (stomping GROUNDS). The position is not computable from syllable count and the list is selected for words that differ from Mainland English, so it cannot be read as fixed-final stress.
3802.srule: Not mentioned in Murphy 2013 (Sec. 1.8.4 'Word Stress' p. 24, Sec. 2.4.3 pp. 48-50, pp. 130-133, 252 read; the word 'secondary' does not occur in the dissertation). Table 1.3 marks one stressed syllable per word.

tn.quote: Pitch accents are represented through the use of a single H (high) or L (low) tone or a combination of the two. It is the overall height of the utterance in HCE and Hawaiian that indicates whether the utterance is a question or statement.
